newsitem.title: USA: Analysts looking for Blockbuster's direction.
newsitem.headline: Analysts looking for Blockbuster's direction.

text.p: Viacom Inc will hold its first talk with analysts since replacing the head of its high-profile Blockbuster unit, and Wall Street is hoping for a clearer picture on the unit's direction and its cost-cutting efforts after the call Wednesday afternoon.
Earlier Wednesday, Viacom reported an operating loss of $0.11 a share, compared to a profit of $0.01 a share and narrower than the First Call mean estimate of a $0.16 a share loss.
Viacom was to hold a conference call with analysts at 1400 EDT to outline its first quarter earnings. Analysts said they were most interested in hearing what Viacom had to say about Blockbuster.
Several weeks after Blockbuster Chairman and Chief Executive Bill Fields resigned analysts said it remains uncertain what Viacom plans for Blockbuster.
Under Fields, Blockbuster was moving toward offering a greater variety of products besides videos, prominently displaying popcorn and movie-related toys.
It now appears as though Viacom executives are looking to retreat from that strategy and focus on the video-rental business.

"What we're looking for is a sense the company has some control over the budgeting" and direction of the unit, Paine Webber analyst Chris Dixon said. "What we're going on right now is some confusion."
Viacom was planning an afternoon conference call with analysts in the afternoon, coming hours after it released its first quarter earnings that were in largely in line with analysts' expecations.
In early afternoon trading, Viacom's stock was up 1/2 to 28-3/4, and just 47,300 shares had changed hands. Its class B shares were up 7/16 to 28-15/16 with 414,600 shares being traded.
In the first quarter, Viacom reported a net loss from continuing operations of $23.8 million, or $0.11 per share, on revenues of $2.9 billion.
In the prior year's quarter, Viacom reported a profit from continuing operations of $19.4 million, or $0.01 per share, on revenues of $2.6 billion.
The First Call consensus estimate for this year's quarter was a loss of $0.16 per share.

Viacom had forewarned analysts that earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization in the Blockbuster unit would be down between 15 percent and 16 percent. In fact, the drop in EBITDA -- known as operating cash flow among media companies -- was about 15 percent.
"It wasn't a tremendous quarter, but the die had already been cast for that," Nesbitt Burns analyst James Goss said.

The question mark remains at the company's Blockbuster unit, which has been a troubling segment since it was merged into Viacom in 1994, largely because of softness in the video rental market, analysts said.
Fields, a former Wal-Mart Stores Inc executive who left Blockbuster last month, has since joined Hudson's Bay Co. His background was in retail and that's the style he brought to Blockbuster.
Since his departure, Viacom Chairman and Chief Executive Sumner Redstone and Deputy Chairman Tom Dooley have been overseeing Blockbuster's operations.
And instead of emphasizing the general entertainment products, Redstone and Dooley now are looking to focus on Blockbuster's core product: video rentals.
A spokeswoman said that although general merchandise would still be available at Blockbuster, it is unlikely they would remain so prominently displayed.
Several analysts said Wednesday that the mixed signals were unsettling, but that they were heartened that Blockbuster may return to focusing on video rentals.
"There was a mixed reception to what (Fields) was doing anyhow," NatWest Securities analyst Gary Farber said.

Offered Nesbitt Burns' Goss: "The dynamics of running a diversified retail outlet ... are different from running a video-rental business, where the profitability is higher. I don't think you really want to have a feel of a convenience store."

Still, most analysts said they simply want clear direction from the company to instill any confidence in the unit. Analysts said they are particularly interested in knowing when the company plans to find a successor to Fields.

"It's very unclear what new direction Blockbuster will take," Smith Barney analyst Jill Krutick said, adding that she is looking for "confidence that things are building up as anticipated or that they're getting their arms around Blockbuster."
